content_voiceover: So if routine PT and aPTT are unreliable for DOACs, what should we actually use to monitor them? This slide lists the specific options. Mass spectrometry, typically liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry, is the gold standard, giving a precise plasma drug concentration, but it is not widely available and turnaround time is far too slow for urgent clinical decisions, so it is mainly a research or reference lab tool. For direct thrombin inhibitors like dabigatran, the useful functional assays are the dilute thrombin time, sometimes called the Hemoclot assay, which has a linear relationship across the clinical concentration range, and the ecarin clotting time, which uses ecarin venom to generate thrombin in a reaction that is directly inhibited by the drug. For direct factor Xa inhibitors, meaning rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, and betrixaban, the chromogenic anti-Xa assay calibrated with drug specific standards is the test of choice. This is conceptually similar to how we monitor low molecular weight heparin with anti-Xa assays, but you must use a calibrator specific to that particular DOAC, because a heparin calibrated anti-Xa assay will not give an accurate result.
keypoints: Mass spectrometry is the gold standard but impractical for routine urgent use
Dilute thrombin time and ecarin clotting time assess direct thrombin inhibitors
Drug specific chromogenic anti-Xa assay quantifies factor Xa inhibitor levels
Standard PT and aPTT are not adequate substitutes for these specific assays
keypoint_voiceover: Mass spectrometry is the gold standard for DOAC quantification but too slow for routine clinical use. Direct thrombin inhibitors like dabigatran are assessed with dilute thrombin time or ecarin clotting time. Factor Xa inhibitors need a drug specific chromogenic anti-Xa assay. Standard PT and aPTT are not adequate substitutes for any of these.
